newsitem.title: JAPAN: DVD sales off to slow start in Japan.
newsitem.headline: DVD sales off to slow start in Japan.

text.p: A new digital video player meant to revolutionise the entertainment world made a quiet, wet debut in heavy rain in Japan on Friday, with consumers throwing a curious look at the product while few bothered to open up their purses.

The digital video disc, DVD, is expected eventually to sweep away prerecorded video movies, compact discs (CDs) and CD-ROMs. A DVD resembles an audio CD but can hold up to 14 times as much information.

At Tokyo's busy Akihabara district, where nearly 300 electronic gadget shops are located, few retailers put up special DVD sales corners due to a delay in shipments and a lack of software titles, marking a slow sales start.
"With only two or three DVD models available, gorgeous displays and campaigns are impossible," said a retailer, waiting for customers in the rain.
"I would buy one, but not now," said a tourist from Canada. "This is small and better than the laser disc, but I'm not familiar with the machine yet," he said.
The units cost around 78,000 yen ($680) each.
A group of the world's top ten electronics and film makers that developed the DVD originally planned to start selling the players in late summer.

But tangled negotiations with the Hollywood studios on copy protection measures delayed the launch, and only two makers -- Toshiba Corp and Matsushita Electric Industrial Co -- were ready to start selling DVDs on the official launch day.
Some consumers said they would wait until a rewritable DVD disc is put on sale -- probably late next year.
"Pre-recorded discs are not particularly appealing," said a student. "But it would be great if you can record your favourite films on the disc as many times as you want."
The hastened launch of the player, aimed at the lucrative Christmas sales season, also meant there were few software titles available.
On Friday, only three software titles, mostly music videos, were on sale as some software makers put off the release for one or two weeks due to technical problems.
Both Matsushita and Toshiba say 40 or 50 titles will be on sale by the end of this year, but others aren't too sure.
"That seems a bit too optimistic," said a spokesman for Pioneer Electronic Corp.
"The game won't start until the weekend," said an official at Matsushita Electric, who was scouting the stores to see how things were going. ($=114 yen)
